units.title: Rights and the States
units.blurb: Barron and the original Bill of Rights, the Slaughter-House Cases, incorporation through due process, and the state action requirement.

units.title: Due Process
units.blurb: Procedural due process, the Lochner era and its end, the methods judges use to identify unenumerated rights, family and autonomy, and the abortion and marriage cases in strictly legal terms.

units.title: Equal Protection
units.blurb: The framework and rational basis, race and strict scrutiny from Plessy to Brown, discriminatory purpose, affirmative action, sex and other classifications, and fundamental rights under equal protection.

units.title: Freedom of Speech and Press
units.blurb: From clear and present danger to Brandenburg, content-based and content-neutral laws, unprotected categories, symbolic speech, defamation, prior restraint, public forums, students and public employees, money in politics, and compelled speech and association.

units.title: The Religion Clauses
units.blurb: The Establishment Clause and its tests, school prayer, aid to religious schools, free exercise from Sherbert to Smith and after, and RFRA. Taught as law, not theology.

units.title: The Second Amendment
units.blurb: Heller and McDonald, and the limits on the right that the Court has described.

units.title: Criminal Procedure
units.blurb: Searches and seizures, warrants and their exceptions, the exclusionary rule, Miranda, self-incrimination and double jeopardy, counsel, juries and confrontation, and the Eighth Amendment.

units.title: Property and Voting
units.blurb: The Takings Clause and voting rights law.

topics.title: The Bill of Rights and the States
topics.short: In Barron v. Baltimore (1833) Chief Justice Marshall held that the Bill of Rights limited only the federal government, so Baltimore owed no just compensation under the Fifth Amendment for ruining a wharf.
topics.trouble: Students assume the Bill of Rights always bound the states. Before the Fourteenth Amendment, citizens relied on state constitutions for protection against states.

topics.title: The Slaughter-House Cases
topics.short: In the Slaughter-House Cases (1873), 5 to 4, the Court read the Fourteenth Amendment's Privileges or Immunities Clause narrowly, covering only rights of national citizenship, which left that clause largely unused (Saenz v. Roe, 1999, is a rare exception).
topics.trouble: Students confuse the Fourteenth Amendment's Privileges or Immunities Clause with Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause. Article IV concerns treatment of out-of-state citizens; the Fourteenth's clause concerns rights of U.S. citizenship.

topics.title: Selective Incorporation
topics.short: Through the Due Process Clause the Court has applied most Bill of Rights guarantees to the states, asking whether a right is fundamental to "our scheme of ordered liberty" and "deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition" (Duncan v. Louisiana, 1968; McDonald v. Chicago, 2010; Timbs v. Indiana, 2019; Ramos v. Louisiana, 2020).
topics.trouble: Students think incorporation came through the Privileges or Immunities Clause. The Court used the Due Process Clause; in McDonald only Justice Thomas would have used Privileges or Immunities.

topics.title: State Action
topics.short: The Fourteenth Amendment limits states, not private persons (the Civil Rights Cases, 1883); private conduct counts as state action when it performs a traditional public function (Marsh v. Alabama, 1946), when courts enforce it (Shelley v. Kraemer, 1948) or when the state is entangled with it (Burton v. Wilmington Parking Authority, 1961).
topics.trouble: Students think any regulated or licensed business is a state actor. Regulation and public money alone are not enough (Jackson v. Metropolitan Edison, 1974); look for public function, entanglement or enforcement.

topics.title: Procedural Due Process
topics.short: When government deprives a person of a protected life, liberty or property interest (Board of Regents v. Roth, 1972), it must give fair procedure; Goldberg v. Kelly (1970) required a hearing before welfare benefits end, and Mathews v. Eldridge (1976) weighs the private interest, the risk of error and the government's interest.
topics.trouble: Students think due process always requires a full trial. The process due depends on the Mathews balance; often notice and a chance to respond are enough.

topics.title: The Lochner Era
topics.short: In Lochner v. New York (1905), 5 to 4, the Court struck down a maximum-hours law for bakers as violating liberty of contract; Justice Holmes's dissent said the Constitution "does not enact Mr. Herbert Spencer's Social Statics"; the Court upheld some laws (Muller v. Oregon, 1908) and struck down others (Adkins, 1923).
topics.trouble: Students think the Court struck down every labor law of the era. It upheld many, including hours limits in mines (Holden v. Hardy, 1898) and for women (Muller).

topics.title: The End of Economic Due Process
topics.short: Nebbia v. New York (1934) and West Coast Hotel v. Parrish (1937), which overruled Adkins, ended close review of economic regulation; since then such laws get rational basis review.
topics.trouble: Students think substantive due process ended in 1937. Its economic branch receded; its protection of personal and family rights continued and grew.

topics.title: Finding Unenumerated Rights: Two Methods
topics.short: Washington v. Glucksberg (1997) asks for a "careful description" of the asserted right and whether it is deeply rooted in the Nation's history and tradition; another approach, from Justice Harlan's dissent in Poe v. Ullman (1961) and used in Obergefell (2015), treats tradition as a living one and reasons from principle.
topics.trouble: Students treat one method as the law's clear answer. Present each in its best form: Glucksberg's supporters stress restraint and democratic choice; its critics say a narrow description of the right can decide the case in advance.

topics.title: Family and Personal Autonomy
topics.short: The Court has protected parents' rights to direct their children's upbringing (Meyer v. Nebraska, 1923; Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 1925; Troxel v. Granville, 2000), extended family living together (Moore v. East Cleveland, 1977) and married couples' use of contraceptives (Griswold v. Connecticut, 1965).
topics.trouble: Students think Griswold rested on a clause that names privacy. Justice Douglas found "penumbras" of several amendments; concurring justices relied on the Ninth Amendment or on due process.

topics.title: The Abortion Cases: Legal History
topics.short: Roe v. Wade (1973) held that due process protects a right to choose abortion, with a trimester framework; Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992) kept Roe's central holding and adopted an "undue burden" test; the Court overruled both in 2022.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the tests and the cases. Roe: trimesters; Casey: undue burden.

topics.title: Liberty, Marriage and the Right to Refuse Treatment
topics.short: Loving v. Virginia (1967) struck down bans on interracial marriage; Lawrence v. Texas (2003) struck down a state law criminalizing private conduct between consenting adults of the same sex, overruling Bowers v. Hardwick (1986); Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) held same-sex couples may marry; Cruzan (1990) and Glucksberg (1997) addressed refusing medical treatment and assisted suicide.
topics.trouble: Students think Glucksberg found a right to assisted suicide. It held there is no such fundamental right, though states may choose to allow it; Cruzan assumed a competent person's right to refuse treatment.

topics.title: The Equal Protection Framework
topics.short: Equal protection analysis asks what classification a law makes and then applies the matching tier; the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause imposes the same requirement on the federal government (Bolling v. Sharpe, 1954).
topics.trouble: Students think the Equal Protection Clause applies to the federal government by its words. It names the states; Bolling reached federal action through the Fifth Amendment ("reverse incorporation").

topics.title: Rational Basis in Equal Protection
topics.short: Most classifications get rational basis review and are upheld (Railway Express Agency v. New York, 1949); a few laws have failed it when they rested on animus or irrational prejudice (City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 1985; Romer v. Evans, 1996).
topics.trouble: Students think rational basis means automatic approval. It almost always does, but Cleburne and Romer show it can fail where a law's only apparent purpose is dislike of a group.

topics.title: Race and Strict Scrutiny
topics.short: Racial classifications get strict scrutiny: Strauder v. West Virginia (1880) struck down excluding Black men from juries; Korematsu (1944) upheld the wartime exclusion order and has since been repudiated; Loving (1967) struck down interracial marriage bans.
topics.trouble: Students think Korematsu applied rational basis. The Court said racial restrictions are "immediately suspect" and get "the most rigid scrutiny," and still upheld the order; it is now cited as a warning.

topics.title: From Plessy to Brown
topics.short: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld "separate but equal"; the NAACP's cases (Missouri ex rel. Gaines, 1938; Sweatt v. Painter, 1950) found separate graduate schools unequal; Brown v. Board of Education (1954), unanimous, held separate schools "inherently unequal," and Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed."
topics.trouble: Students think Brown overruled Plessy everywhere at once. Brown addressed public education; later per curiam orders applied it to beaches, buses, parks and other public facilities.

topics.title: Discriminatory Purpose and Effect
topics.short: A law neutral on its face violates equal protection only if adopted with discriminatory purpose (Washington v. Davis, 1976; Arlington Heights, 1977, listing evidence of purpose); a disparate impact alone is not enough, though some statutes reach impact; Yick Wo v. Hopkins (1886) struck down discriminatory enforcement.
topics.trouble: Students think unequal results prove a constitutional violation. Under the Constitution purpose must be shown; disparate impact matters under some statutes, such as Title VII.

topics.title: Race-Conscious Admissions and Programs
topics.short: Regents v. Bakke (1978) barred quotas but allowed race as one factor; Croson (1989) and Adarand (1995) applied strict scrutiny to all racial classifications, including remedial ones; Grutter v. Bollinger (2003) upheld a holistic program and Gratz v. Bollinger (2003) struck down automatic points; the Court rejected race-conscious admissions programs in 2023.
topics.trouble: Students describe the cases through one side's view. Supporters stressed diversity and remedying past discrimination; opponents stressed that the Constitution forbids sorting by race. Report each opinion's reasoning and the holding.

topics.title: Sex Discrimination
topics.short: Reed v. Reed (1971) struck down a preference for men as estate administrators; Frontiero (1973) drew a plurality for strict scrutiny; Craig v. Boren (1976) set intermediate scrutiny; United States v. Virginia (1996) required an "exceedingly persuasive justification" to exclude women from VMI.
topics.trouble: Students think sex classifications get strict scrutiny. Frontiero's call for it drew only four votes; the standard is intermediate scrutiny, as sharpened in United States v. Virginia.

topics.title: Other Classifications
topics.short: State laws discriminating against lawfully present noncitizens usually get strict scrutiny (Graham v. Richardson, 1971); classifications by legitimacy get intermediate scrutiny; age (Massachusetts Board of Retirement v. Murgia, 1976), wealth (San Antonio v. Rodriguez, 1973) and disability (Cleburne) get rational basis.
topics.trouble: Students think every disadvantaged group gets heightened scrutiny. The Court has declined to add new suspect classes since the 1970s; age, wealth and disability get rational basis.

topics.title: Fundamental Rights and Equal Protection
topics.short: Laws burdening fundamental rights unequally get strict scrutiny: Reynolds v. Sims (1964) required "one person, one vote" for state legislatures; Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections (1966) struck down poll taxes in state elections; Shapiro v. Thompson (1969) and Saenz v. Roe (1999) protected the right to travel; Bush v. Gore (2000) ended the Florida recount.
topics.trouble: Students think education is a fundamental right under the federal Constitution. Rodriguez (1973) held it is not, though many state constitutions protect it.

topics.title: From Clear and Present Danger
topics.short: Schenck v. United States (1919) upheld convictions for antidraft leaflets under a "clear and present danger" test; Holmes's dissent in Abrams (1919) and Brandeis's concurrence in Whitney (1927) argued for a narrower test; Dennis v. United States (1951) upheld Communist Party leaders' convictions.
topics.trouble: Students quote "falsely shouting fire in a theatre" as the law. It was an analogy in Schenck; the test Schenck applied has since been replaced by Brandenburg.

topics.title: Brandenburg v. Ohio
topics.short: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) held that the government may not punish advocacy of force or lawbreaking unless it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce it; it overruled Whitney.
topics.trouble: Students leave out one of the elements. All three are needed: intent (directed to), imminence, and likelihood.

topics.title: Content-Based and Content-Neutral Laws
topics.short: Laws that regulate speech because of its subject or message are content-based and get strict scrutiny (Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 2015); content-neutral laws get intermediate scrutiny; viewpoint discrimination is the most suspect of all.
topics.trouble: Students think a law that treats all viewpoints equally is content-neutral. A law can be viewpoint-neutral yet content-based if it singles out a subject (all political signs, for example).

topics.title: Categories of Unprotected Speech
topics.short: A few narrow categories get little or no protection: incitement, true threats (Virginia v. Black, 2003), fighting words (Chaplinsky, 1942), obscenity (Miller v. California, 1973), defamation and fraud; the Court has refused to add new categories (United States v. Stevens, 2010).
topics.trouble: Students think "hate speech" is an unprotected category. The Court has not recognized it as one; speech in such cases is unprotected only if it fits a category such as true threats or incitement.

topics.title: Symbolic Speech
topics.short: Conduct meant to communicate can be speech: United States v. O'Brien (1968) upheld a ban on burning draft cards under a four-part test for content-neutral rules; Tinker (1969) protected armbands; Texas v. Johnson (1989) protected flag burning as political expression.
topics.trouble: Students think O'Brien means symbolic speech is unprotected. O'Brien gives intermediate review when a law targets conduct for reasons unrelated to its message; Johnson shows the result changes when the law targets the message.

topics.title: New York Times v. Sullivan
topics.short: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964) held that a public official suing for defamation must prove "actual malice" (knowing falsity or reckless disregard for the truth); Gertz v. Robert Welch (1974) let states set a lower standard for private figures.
topics.trouble: Students think "actual malice" means ill will toward the person. It is a term of art about the speaker's knowledge of falsity, not about hatred or spite.

topics.title: Prior Restraint
topics.short: Orders that stop speech before it happens bear a heavy presumption against validity: Near v. Minnesota (1931) struck down a law allowing newspapers to be shut down; New York Times Co. v. United States (1971), the Pentagon Papers case, refused to block publication.
topics.trouble: Students think the Pentagon Papers decision was one opinion of the Court. It was a short per curiam with nine separate opinions; it says the government did not meet its heavy burden.

topics.title: Public Forums
topics.short: Streets and parks are traditional public forums; government may open designated or limited forums; in nonpublic forums restrictions need only be reasonable and viewpoint-neutral (Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators' Association, 1983).
topics.trouble: Students think all government property is a public forum. A military base or an airport terminal is not; the forum category sets the test.

topics.title: Time, Place and Manner
topics.short: In public forums, content-neutral rules on time, place and manner are valid if narrowly tailored to a significant government interest and leaving open ample alternative channels (Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 1989); they need not be the least restrictive means.
topics.trouble: Students apply strict scrutiny's "least restrictive means" to these rules. Ward says a time, place and manner rule need not be the least restrictive means.

topics.title: Students, Public Employees and Government Speech
topics.short: Tinker (1969) protects student speech unless it would substantially disrupt school; Bethel (1986), Hazelwood (1988) and Morse (2007) define limits; public employees' speech as citizens on public concerns is protected (Pickering, 1968) but not speech made pursuant to official duties (Garcetti v. Ceballos, 2006).
topics.trouble: Students think Tinker lets schools punish any speech some people dislike. The test is substantial disruption, judged on facts; the exceptions for lewd, school-sponsored and drug-promoting speech are narrow.

topics.title: Campaign Finance and Speech
topics.short: Buckley v. Valeo (1976) upheld limits on contributions but struck down limits on independent expenditures; Citizens United v. FEC (2010), 5 to 4, held corporations and unions may spend independently on elections; disclosure rules have mostly been upheld.
topics.trouble: Students think Buckley treated contributions and expenditures the same. It distinguished them: contribution limits survive more easily because of the risk of corruption.

topics.title: Compelled Speech and Association
topics.short: Government may not compel people to salute the flag (West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943, overruling Gobitis) or display a state motto (Wooley v. Maynard, 1977); NAACP v. Alabama (1958) protected the privacy of membership lists; Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian, and Bisexual Group of Boston (1995) and Boy Scouts of America v. Dale (2000) protected a parade's message and a group's expressive association.
topics.trouble: Students think Barnette rested on religious freedom. Though the families were Jehovah's Witnesses, the Court rested on freedom of speech: "no official, high or petty, can prescribe what shall be orthodox."

topics.title: The Establishment Clause
topics.short: Everson v. Board of Education (1947) applied the Establishment Clause to the states, invoking Jefferson's "wall of separation," while upholding bus fare reimbursement for students at religious schools.
topics.trouble: Students think the phrase "separation of church and state" is in the Constitution. It comes from Jefferson's 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists; the Constitution's words are "no law respecting an establishment of religion."

topics.title: Establishment Tests
topics.short: Lemon v. Kurtzman (1971) asked about secular purpose, primary effect and excessive entanglement; the Court also used endorsement and coercion tests (Lee v. Weisman, 1992) and, for legislative prayer and old monuments, history and tradition (Marsh v. Chambers, 1983); the Court said in 2022 that it no longer applies the Lemon test.
topics.trouble: Students treat the tests as one test. Lemon asks about purpose, effect and entanglement; endorsement about a reasonable observer; coercion about pressure to take part; history about long tradition.

topics.title: Prayer in Public Schools
topics.short: Engel v. Vitale (1962) struck down a state-composed prayer; Abington v. Schempp (1963) struck down school-sponsored Bible reading; Lee v. Weisman (1992) and Santa Fe v. Doe (2000) struck down prayers at graduation and football games; private prayer by students is protected.
topics.trouble: Students think students may not pray at public school. The cases bar school-sponsored prayer; private prayer by students is protected.

topics.title: Public Aid and Religious Schools
topics.short: Zelman v. Simmons-Harris (2002) upheld vouchers chosen by parents; Trinity Lutheran (2017) and Espinoza (2020) held that a state that funds private schools or programs may not exclude religious ones because they are religious.
topics.trouble: Students think the Establishment Clause forbids any public money from reaching religious schools. Aid through parents' independent choices is allowed, and excluding religious schools from a general program can violate Free Exercise.

topics.title: Free Exercise
topics.short: Sherbert v. Verner (1963) and Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) applied strict scrutiny to burdens on religion; Employment Division v. Smith (1990) held neutral, generally applicable laws need no exemption; Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. Hialeah (1993) struck down laws that targeted a faith and were not generally applicable.
topics.trouble: Students think Smith lets government target religion. Laws that single out religious practice still get strict scrutiny (Lukumi); Smith concerns neutral, generally applicable laws.

topics.title: RFRA
topics.short: Congress answered Smith with the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993), restoring strict scrutiny for substantial burdens on religion; City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) held it invalid as applied to states, but it binds the federal government (Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, 2014).
topics.trouble: Students think Boerne struck down RFRA entirely. It struck it down as applied to states; federal law remains subject to RFRA, and many states have their own versions.

topics.title: Heller and McDonald
topics.short: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), 5 to 4, held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms, struck down a handgun ban and said some longstanding regulations remain lawful; McDonald v. Chicago (2010) incorporated the right against the states.
topics.trouble: Students state the militia clause's role as settled before Heller. The majority read the prefatory clause as announcing a purpose; Justice Stevens's dissent read the right as tied to militia service. Present both readings.

topics.title: Limits on the Second Amendment Right
topics.short: Heller (2008) called longstanding prohibitions presumptively lawful (possession by felons and the mentally ill, carrying in sensitive places, conditions on commercial sale) and protected arms in common use, not dangerous and unusual ones; Caetano v. Massachusetts (2016) applied Heller to stun guns; since 2022 the Court has judged gun laws by the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation rather than by tiers of scrutiny.
topics.trouble: Students think Heller struck down all gun laws, or that it let governments ban any weapon. It named longstanding regulations as presumptively lawful and protected arms in common use.

topics.title: What Is a Search?
topics.short: Under Katz v. United States (1967) a search occurs when government intrudes on a reasonable expectation of privacy; United States v. Jones (2012) revived a trespass test for physical intrusions; Carpenter v. United States (2018) required a warrant for historical cell-site location records.
topics.trouble: Students think anything a person shares with a third party is never protected. That was the third-party doctrine (Smith v. Maryland, 1979), but Carpenter declined to extend it to cell-site location records.

topics.title: Warrants and Their Exceptions
topics.short: Searches generally need a warrant based on probable cause, but there are exceptions: consent, plain view, search incident to arrest (Chimel, 1969), the automobile exception (Carroll, 1925), exigent circumstances, and brief stops and frisks on reasonable suspicion (Terry v. Ohio, 1968).
topics.trouble: Students confuse probable cause with reasonable suspicion. Reasonable suspicion (for a Terry stop) is a lower standard than probable cause (for an arrest or a warrant).

topics.title: The Exclusionary Rule
topics.short: Evidence from unconstitutional searches is generally excluded at trial: Weeks (1914) in federal court, Mapp v. Ohio (1961) in state courts; exceptions include good-faith reliance on a warrant (United States v. Leon, 1984), independent source and inevitable discovery.
topics.trouble: Students think an illegal search ends the case. Only the tainted evidence is excluded, and the exceptions often let it in.

topics.title: Miranda v. Arizona
topics.short: Miranda v. Arizona (1966) requires police to warn a person in custody before interrogation of the right to remain silent and to a lawyer; Dickerson v. United States (2000) held Miranda is a constitutional rule Congress cannot overrule by statute.
topics.trouble: Students think Miranda applies whenever police speak with someone. It applies to custodial interrogation: both custody and questioning are required.

topics.title: Self-Incrimination and Double Jeopardy
topics.short: No one may be compelled to be a witness against himself in a criminal case; double jeopardy bars a second prosecution for the same offense by the same sovereign after acquittal or conviction, though separate sovereigns (state and federal) may each prosecute (Gamble v. United States, 2019).
topics.trouble: Students think the privilege covers physical evidence such as fingerprints or blood samples. It protects testimonial communication, not physical evidence.

topics.title: The Right to Counsel
topics.short: Powell v. Alabama (1932) required counsel in a capital case; Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), overruling Betts v. Brady, required states to provide counsel to poor defendants charged with felonies; Strickland v. Washington (1984) set the test for ineffective assistance: deficient performance and prejudice.
topics.trouble: Students think Gideon required lawyers in every case. It covered felonies; Argersinger (1972) and later cases extended it to misdemeanors that result in imprisonment.

topics.title: Juries and Confrontation
topics.short: Duncan v. Louisiana (1968) incorporated the jury trial right for serious crimes; Ramos v. Louisiana (2020) required unanimous juries in state felony trials; Batson v. Kentucky (1986) barred race-based jury strikes; Crawford v. Washington (2004) requires that testimonial statements be tested by cross-examination.
topics.trouble: Students think the Sixth Amendment guarantees a jury in every criminal case. It applies to serious offenses; petty offenses (generally six months or less) may be tried without a jury.

topics.title: The Eighth Amendment
topics.short: The Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail and fines and cruel and unusual punishments: Furman v. Georgia (1972) halted death sentences under existing laws, Gregg v. Georgia (1976) upheld revised procedures, and the Court has barred the death penalty for people with intellectual disabilities (Atkins, 2002) and for those under 18 at the time of the crime (Roper, 2005); Timbs (2019) incorporated the Excessive Fines Clause.
topics.trouble: Students think Furman abolished the death penalty. It struck down the way it was then imposed; Gregg upheld revised statutes four years later.

topics.title: Takings
topics.short: The Fifth Amendment requires just compensation when property is taken for public use; Kelo v. City of New London (2005), 5 to 4, held economic development a public use; regulations can be takings if they go "too far": Penn Central (1978) balances factors, and Lucas (1992) treats a total loss of economic value as a taking.
topics.trouble: Students think Kelo let governments take property without paying. Compensation was required; the question was whether the taking was for a "public use." Many states narrowed eminent domain after Kelo.

topics.title: Voting Rights Law
topics.short: Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act bars voting practices that result in denying or abridging the vote on account of race; Thornburg v. Gingles (1986) set the preconditions for vote dilution claims; Shelby County v. Holder (2013) struck down the preclearance coverage formula; Rucho (2019) left partisan gerrymandering claims to the political process and state courts.
topics.trouble: Students mix up racial and partisan gerrymandering claims. Racial claims can be heard in federal court under the Constitution and the VRA; after Rucho, purely partisan claims cannot.
